paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis caused by PNPLA8 mutation is an autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder. Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) noted that 3 presentations of biallelic PNPLA8 variants had been described: a congenital form with congenital microcephaly, early-onset epileptic encephalopathy and early death; childhood neurodegeneration with progressive microcephaly; and adult-onset cerebellar ataxia with peripheral neuropathy. Nakamura et al. (2024) concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease forms a continuum, ranging from developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with congenital microcephaly to childhood-onset neurodegeneration.

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) described the clinical, biochemical and pathologic findings in a 23-year-old man with a mitochondrial myopathy. He had had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy that caused cardiac insufficiency 22 years before the skeletal myopathy presented. Venous lactate levels were elevated, and at one stage of the illness he developed severe lactic acidosis. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids, which was confirmed by histochemistry and by thin-layer chromatography.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a girl (CMH193) whose toe-walking was noted in her first year. She had a positive Gowers sign at age 2 years and could no longer walk by age 3 years. She was last reported at age 7 years. Her features included progressive muscle weakness, hypotonia, complex partial seizures, poor weight gain, a lean body habitus, dystonia, dysarthria, dysmetria, spasticity, and tight heel cords. Laboratory studies showed lactic acidosis, an elevated anion gap, elevated blood pyruvate, and a deficiency of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate in the CSF. Brain MRI showed increased signal in the medial globus pallidus. On muscle biopsy, fiber size varied and some fibers were atrophic. There were no ragged-red fibers. Electron microscopy showed abnormal mitochondrial cristae, osmiophilic inclusions, and subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria. Creatine phosphokinase and respiratory chain function were not abnormal.

paragraphs.text: Shukla et al. (2018) described 2 unrelated girls with biallelic PNPLA8 loss-of-function variants. Their features varied but were similar, and included microcephaly, severe global developmental delay, spasticity, lactic acidosis, and progressive cerebellar atrophy. The authors considered the condition a progressive neurodegenerative mitochondrial disorder. Patient 1 was the second child of consanguineous Indian parents. She had a low birth weight and was evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit on her sixth day of life for congenital microcephaly and seizures. She had multifocal clonic neonatal seizures, spasticity of all 4 limbs, and overriding cranial sutures. Brain MRI showed microcephaly with a simplified gyral pattern, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, a prominent cisterna magna with a hypoplastic cerebellum, and brainstem atrophy. MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak.

paragraphs.text: Patient 2 of Shukla et al. (2018) was a girl of Indian/Fijian ancestry born to nonconsanguineous parents. She developed normally until 13 months of age and then regressed. She was last reported at age 15 years. She had epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures, severe global developmental delay, no speech, and required gastrostomy tube feeding. Other findings included central hypotonia, acquired microcephaly, choreiform movements, dystonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent muscle stretch reflexes, spasticity, and joint contractures. EEG showed multifocal epileptiform discharges with background slowing, and visual evoked potentials were abnormal. Brain MRI showed delayed myelination, progressive cerebellar atrophy, brainstem and cerebral atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum. MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak. Electron microscopy of muscle showed enlarged, irregular mitochondria, but respiratory chain complex I to IV activities were normal. Echocardiography detected hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis. Blood lactate was elevated on several occasions, and GDF15 was also elevated. She also had obstructive sleep apnea and restrictive lung disease.

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) described a milder phenotype in 2 Lithuanian adult sibs. Both had adolescent-onset cerebellar ataxia and sensorimotor polyneuropathy, which advanced markedly in the teens but progressed only slightly in adulthood. Cognition was preserved, and there was no visual, auditory, cardiac, or liver dysfunction. Sibling A, a man last reported at age 49 years, first developed lower limb weakness and distal muscle atrophy at age 14 years. His later findings included axial ataxia, tetraparesis, decreased muscle tone, absent lower limb tendon reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, dysmetria, length-dependent hypoesthesia in the lower limbs, and a sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. He became nonambulant at age 44 years. At age 45 years he had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus. Imaging showed mild cerebellar atrophy. Sibling B, his sister, was last reported at age 21 years. She developed difficulty walking and weakness of both lower limbs at age 14 years. Her findings included distal muscle atrophy of the upper and lower limbs, absent lower limb tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, severe axial ataxia, and appendicular dysmetria that was more pronounced in the lower limbs. She was unable to maintain an upright posture. Her cranial nerve examination and cognitive evaluation were normal, and EMG showed no myopathic changes.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 new patients with biallelic PNPLA8 variants and reviewed a total of 25 affected individuals from 20 families. Among the 14 new patients, central hypotonia was present in 13 of 13, dystonia in 8 of 12, seizures in 10 of 14, and cerebellar atrophy in 12 of 12. Eight patients (families 1 through 8) were severely affected. They came from Japan (patients 1 and 2, nonconsanguineous) and from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Turkey, and Lebanon (patients 3 through 8, all consanguineous). Families 7 and 8 had been reported previously. These patients had congenital microcephaly (5 of 7), progressive microcephaly, no developmental milestones, severe intellectual disability, and spasticity. They had early-onset seizures, beginning at 1 day of age in patients 1, 2, 3, and 8, at 2 days in patient 6, at 1 month in patient 7, at 3 months in patient 5, and at 7 months in patient 4. Imaging showed a simplified gyral pattern, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and progressive cerebral atrophy. Patient 1 died at age 4 years, patient 2 at 10 months, and patient 8 at 8 months. Two patients (families 9 and 10) had disease of intermediate severity, with cerebellar atrophy that was very mild in patient 10. Four patients (families 11 and 12) had relatively mild features. All 4 attained walking and later regressed, 3 of 4 had ataxia, 3 of 4 had mild or no intellectual disability, and all 4 had a single seizure or none. These mild patients included 3 Iranian sibs from a consanguineous family (patients 11a, 11b, and 11c), who had hypotonia, dystonia, ataxia, and a neuromuscular disorder. Patient 11b had seizures from age 31 years. The fourth was an Egyptian woman born to consanguineous parents (patient 12), last reported at age 21 years, who had developmental delay with regression after walking, mild intellectual disability, hypotonia, dystonia, a neuromuscular disorder, and cerebellar atrophy.
